subject: Biology
title: Population Growth
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Population Growth.

hook.text: One bacterium becomes two, then four, then eight. Exponential growth can't last forever.

buildup.text: Without limits, a population grows exponentially—doubling at a steady rate over time.

discovery.text: Resources run out. Predators arrive. Disease strikes. Growth slows and levels off.

twist.text: The carrying capacity is the maximum population an environment can sustain long-term.

climax.text: Populations that overshoot their carrying capacity often crash dramatically.

punchline.text: Growth has limits. Nature always collects.

quiz.question: What is carrying capacity?
options: Maximum population an environment can sustain
The rate at which a population grows
The number of species in an area

details.summary: Population growth is governed by birth rates, death rates, immigration, and emigration. Exponential growth occurs when resources are unlimited, but populations inevitably encounter environmental resistance and level off at the carrying capacity of their habitat.
details.whyItMatters: Population dynamics determine whether species thrive or face extinction and how they interact with ecosystems. Understanding growth patterns is essential for wildlife management, conservation planning, and predicting pest outbreaks.
takeaways: Exponential growth produces J-shaped curves in unlimited environments
Logistic growth produces S-shaped curves as populations approach carrying capacity
Carrying capacity depends on available food, water, space, and other resources

faq.question: What is carrying capacity?
faq.answer: Carrying capacity is the maximum population size an environment can sustain indefinitely. It depends on available resources like food, water, and shelter. Populations near carrying capacity experience increased competition, disease, and mortality that slow growth.

faq.question: Can populations exceed their carrying capacity?
faq.answer: Yes, temporarily. Overshoot happens when populations grow past what the environment can sustain, often followed by a crash as resources are depleted. Reindeer on St. Matthew Island increased to 6,000 and then crashed to 42 when food ran out.
